_readme: The Data Sources screen (DataSourcesScreen, src/ui/data_sources/). Edit this file to change it; no code change needed.
groups: shown in order. title, optional note, entries. An entry: name, use (what the game uses it for), link (optional, opens in the browser).
placeholder: true marks a group still to be filled. Its note is shown only while it has no entries; otherwise a note is always shown.
Facts come from game/docs/SCIENCE_AND_DATA.md and CREDITS.md; keep them in step.
title: DATA SOURCES
intro: What in Last Light comes from real data, what comes from published science, and what we made up.

entries.name: LROC NAC DTM of the Apollo 12 landing site (2 m)
entries.use: The ground you drive on: the play area is the measured 2 m elevation posts, unchanged except for the graded base. Slopes, both M3 routes, Head crater and its shade all come from it.

entries.name: LROC Apollo 12 orthophoto
entries.use: An approximate brightness pattern for the ground near the site (not used as albedo).

entries.name: SLDEM2015 (LOLA and SELENE Terrain Camera)
entries.use: The terrain beyond the DTM, out to 33 km from the site, with the Moon’s curvature.

entries.name: Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Head crater
entries.use: The name, position (3.01° S, 23.43° W) and size (120 m) of Head crater, which the short M3 route crosses.

entries.name: LROC coordinates of lunar human features (2016)
entries.use: Where the Apollo 12 lander, the ALSEP and Surveyor 3 stand, so the base and routes keep well clear of them.

entries.name: JPL Horizons
entries.use: The sun, Earth and stars as seen from the site on 20 November 1969, during Apollo 12's second moonwalk.

entries.name: NASA: Moon by the Numbers
entries.use: Lunar gravity (1.62 m/s²) for Kite's weight, wheel loads and rolling resistance, and the length of the lunar day.

entries.name: LRO Diviner instrument
entries.use: Why sun and shade ground temperatures matter. The radiometer readings in the game are simulated, not Diviner data.

entries.name: NASA SVS Deep Star Maps 2020 (ESA/Gaia/DPAC)
entries.use: The star field in the Moon's sky.

entries.name: NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LROC WAC colour)
entries.use: The colour map of the main menu's Moon.

entries.name: Blue Marble: Next Generation (NASA Earth Observatory)
entries.use: Earth in the Moon's sky and in the planet explorer.

entries.name: Mars Viking Global Color Mosaic (USGS Astrogeology)
entries.use: Mars in the planet explorer.

entries.name: Apollo 12 photographs AS12-49-7278 and AS12-48-7136
entries.use: The two history cards on the workshop wall.

entries.name: Wheel sinkage and rolling resistance on the TRI-1 lunar soil simulant
entries.use: Rolling resistance of 0.12 times the weight on loose regolith (measured 0.118 to 0.130 for plain wheels); grip wheels cost more energy, as lugged wheels did in the study.

entries.name: The lunar day
entries.use: About 29.5 Earth days, with about 14.75 days of daylight. It sets how high the sun is in M3 for each lander, and so where Head crater is in shade.

entries.name: Earth-Moon light time
entries.use: Radio takes about 1.3 s each way at the Moon's mean distance of 384,400 km. In the opening dialogue Mira, on Earth, says she and Hana are "about a second behind". Kite is driven from the base next to it, so the game adds no delay to the controls.

entries.name: The lunar atmosphere and weather
entries.use: No air and no wind: dust from wheels and the lander flies in clean arcs and lands within seconds.

entries.name: Henriksen et al. (2017), LROC NAC stereo topography
entries.use: How the Apollo 12 DTM was made, and its accuracy.

entries.name: Barker et al. (2016), SLDEM2015
entries.use: How the LOLA and SELENE elevation model was made.

groups.title: Game assumptions
groups.note: Chosen for play, not measured. Time is compressed: a mission takes minutes, not hours.

entries.name: Always-on electronics: 240 W
entries.use: Kite's computers, radio, cameras and thermal control draw power whenever it is off the pad, moving or not. Real rovers carry a standing load like this; the value is set for balance.

entries.name: Electronics-bay heater: 500 W
entries.use: Runs while Kite is in cold shade with the heater fitted; crossing Head's shade costs about 4 % of the battery.

entries.name: Cold shutdown after 20 s
entries.use: In shade without the thermal cover and heater, Kite's electronics shut down and the emergency recovery brings it home. A rule, not a thermal model.

entries.name: Kite's masses and drive motor
entries.use: A 37 kg chassis plus every fitted part (80 kg as standard), and an ideal DC motor with no regeneration.

entries.name: Cargo landers
entries.use: Courier: 30 kg, arrives on story day 4. Freighter: 40 kg, arrives on day 11. 2 kg of packaging per order; a descent delta-v of 1,900 m/s is shown but not computed.

entries.name: The sun in M3
entries.use: A uniform arc over the daylight half of the lunar day; it ignores the site's latitude and libration.

entries.name: Ground temperatures
entries.use: Simulated: sunlit ground from radiative balance for the sun's height, shaded ground -150 °C.

entries.name: Route flags and the boulder field
entries.use: Added objects. The 2 m DTM can't show boulders, so their positions and sizes are invented.

entries.name: Fictional equipment and organisation
entries.use: Kite, IRIS, the field logger, the outpost, the cargo service and the crew (Hana, Mira, Rafi, Evan) are invented for a 2058 story. No endorsement by NASA or ESA is implied.

groups.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge resources
groups.note: Public NASA material that the game's design follows. NASA does not endorse this game.

entries.name: Design and Develop Science Missions (NASA Systems Engineering Webinar, 2025)
entries.use: The missions follow its four segments: launch (the cargo lander, Courier or Freighter), space (Kite and its loadout), ground (the workshop and mission console) and user (the scientists reading the Downlink report). They also follow its steps from goals to design to verify: each goal leads to a loadout, checked against the forecast before driving out.

entries.name: Concept Maturity Levels (JPL)
entries.use: A mission concept matures in stages, from an idea to a checked design. So does each mission here, from a goal to a loadout the forecast says will work.

entries.name: Mission Design Lab (NASA Goddard)
entries.use: Its trade studies and point designs, with power and thermal among the disciplines, are what the M3 route choice asks of you: the short route with grip wheels, or the long route with the standard battery.

entries.name: Build It Yourself: A Learning Game About Telescopes (NASA Webb)
entries.use: The same idea as this game: the science goal decides the engineering, choices are limited, and the results are explained afterwards (the report's why lines).
